title: Contrastive Learning with Complex Heterogeneity

problem.claim: Real-world data may contain multiple modalities and labels, creating multiple types of complex heterogeneity while labeled information is expensive to obtain.

gap.claim: Existing contrastive learning methods do not address false-negative pairs whose members may share a label and therefore have similar representations.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes a unified heterogeneous learning framework combining weighted unsupervised and weighted supervised contrastive losses to model multiple types of heterogeneity.
The paper provides a theoretical analysis of how false-negative pairs can lead vanilla contrastive learning to a sub-optimal solution.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that experiments on real-world data sets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework for modeling multiple types of heterogeneity.

narrative_sequence.summary: Applications increasingly involve data with complex heterogeneity arising from multiple modalities and labels.
Labeled data are expensive, and existing contrastive learning methods can mishandle false-negative pairs.
The proposed framework combines weighted unsupervised and supervised contrastive losses.
Theoretical analysis motivates similarity-based weight adjustment to mitigate false-negative effects.
Experiments on real-world data sets are reported to demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency.

source_observation.claim: The proposed weighted loss automatically adjusts weights according to the similarity of learned representations.

interpretation.claim: Similarity-aware weighting may reduce the harm caused by treating potentially same-label pairs as negatives.

application.claim: When applying contrastive learning to heterogeneous data with limited labels, consider weighting contrastive pairs using learned-representation similarity.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this weighting strategy works beyond the reported real-world data sets or under different heterogeneity patterns.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the real-world data sets, evaluation metrics, baselines, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not specify the theoretical assumptions, formal guarantees, or computational details of the weighted losses.
